title: Fire Arrows of China
summary: In ancient China, alchemists mixing potions to help people live forever accidentally made a powder that burst into flame. Soldiers tied tubes of this powder to arrows, and the arrows flew off by themselves. These were the first real rockets, and soon they were whooshing across battlefields and lighting up festival skies.

sections.heading: The Alchemists' Kitchen
paragraphs: Picture a quiet mountain workshop in China more than a thousand years ago. Smoke curls from a small furnace. On the shelves are jars of strange minerals: yellow crumbs of sulfur, red lumps of a mineral called realgar, white crystals scraped from the walls of caves and old cellars. A man in robes is grinding something in a stone bowl, mixing, heating, watching and writing notes. He is not trying to invent a weapon. He is trying to make a medicine that will let people live forever.

People like him are called alchemists. In China, many alchemists followed Daoism, a tradition of thought that taught living in harmony with nature, and some of them believed that the right mixture of minerals and herbs could create an elixir of long life or even immortality. Emperors paid for this research, hoping to cheat death. For centuries, alchemists heated, boiled and blended every substance they could find. Sadly, many of their elixirs contained poisons such as mercury and arsenic, and historians think several Chinese emperors may have died from drinking them.

Three ingredients in the alchemists' jars turned out to be very special when put together. The first was saltpeter, the white crystals, which chemists today call potassium nitrate. It forms naturally where plant and animal waste rots into the soil, and in China it could be found as a crust on the ground or on cave walls. Alchemists already used it in medicines and knew it made fires flare up brightly. The second was sulfur, a yellow mineral that burns with a blue flame and a terrible smell. The third was charcoal, made by slowly baking wood with very little air until it turns into light, black, easy-to-burn lumps.

Nobody knows the name of the person who first mixed these together. But by the time of the Tang dynasty, which ruled China from 618 to 907, alchemy books were starting to describe what happened. One text dated to 808 gives a recipe of sulfur, saltpeter and a dried plant called birthwort, which would have provided the carbon that charcoal usually supplies. A little later, probably in the middle of the 9th century, a Daoist book called the Zhenyuan miaodao yaolüe, roughly 'Classified Essentials of the Mysterious Dao of the True Origin of Things', included a list of dangerous recipes that alchemists should avoid. One of them was a warning: some people had heated sulfur, realgar and saltpeter together with honey, and the mixture had burst into flame, burning their hands and faces, and even burning down the whole house.

That is the earliest clear description of something like gunpowder. Instead of a medicine for long life, the alchemists had found one of the most dangerous substances in history. The Chinese name it was given tells you where it came from: huoyao, which means 'fire medicine'. Even today, the Chinese word for gunpowder is still huoyao.

It is worth pausing on how much luck and patient work went into this. The right proportions matter enormously. Too little saltpeter and the mixture just smoulders. The ingredients must be ground very fine and mixed very thoroughly. And saltpeter collected from nature is full of other salts that spoil it, so it has to be purified. Over the next few hundred years, Chinese craftsmen would gradually learn all of these tricks, step by step, by trial and error, and sometimes by painful accident.

sections.heading: How Fire Medicine Works
paragraphs: Why is gunpowder so different from an ordinary fire? Think about a campfire. Wood burns only because oxygen from the air reaches it. Cover a fire with a lid or a blanket and it goes out, because it has used up the oxygen and no more can get in. A fire needs two things: a fuel, like wood, and an oxidizer, something that supplies the oxygen. Normally the oxidizer is simply the air around us.

Gunpowder carries its own oxidizer mixed right inside it. That is the job of the saltpeter. When saltpeter gets hot, it releases oxygen. The charcoal and sulfur are the fuels, and the sulfur also helps the mixture catch fire at a lower temperature and burn faster. Because the oxygen is already mixed in, tiny grain by tiny grain, gunpowder does not have to wait for air to drift in. It can burn incredibly fast, and it can even burn inside a closed tube, underwater or, as people would discover much later, in the airless emptiness of space.

When gunpowder burns, the solid powder turns very quickly into a large amount of extremely hot gas, along with smoke made of tiny solid particles. Gas takes up far more space than solid powder. Squeezed into a small space, that hot gas pushes outward hard in every direction. If the powder is sealed inside a strong container, the pressure builds until the container bursts with a bang. That is an explosion. If one end of the container is open, the gas rushes out of that end in a fierce jet. And that jet, as we will soon see, is what makes a rocket go.

Much later, in Europe, the classic recipe for gunpowder settled at roughly 75 parts saltpeter, 15 parts charcoal and 10 parts sulfur. Early Chinese mixtures often had a lot less saltpeter, around half the mixture. Those weaker powders did not explode well. Instead they fizzed, flared and spat flames, burning fiercely for a few seconds. For a weapon meant to set things on fire, or for a tube that needs to push steadily rather than blow apart, that was actually useful. The history of gunpowder weapons is partly the story of people slowly adding more and more saltpeter, and learning to purify it, until the powder became truly explosive.

So here, at last, is the answer to the great puzzle from the end of the last part. People had wondered how anything could move where there was no air to push on. Gunpowder burns without needing air from outside, and the gas it makes can push a tube forward. Nobody in medieval China was thinking about space, of course. But the key ingredient for every rocket that would ever fly, a propellant that brings its own oxidizer along, had arrived.

sections.heading: A Book of War Secrets: the Wujing Zongyao
paragraphs: In 960, a new dynasty, the Song, took power in China. It would rule, in one form or another, until 1279. The Song era was an age of astonishing invention. Printing with movable type was invented in this period. Magnetic compasses were being used for navigation. Huge cities bustled with markets, restaurants and theatres. But the Song empire also faced dangerous neighbours to the north and west, kingdoms of skilled horse-riding warriors. The Song government needed every advantage it could find, and it took a very close interest in the new fire medicine.

In the year 1044, scholars working for Emperor Renzong of Song finished a giant military encyclopedia called the Wujing Zongyao, which means something like 'Collection of the Most Important Military Techniques'. Its chief compilers were officials named Zeng Gongliang, Ding Du and Yang Weide, and the emperor himself wrote the preface. The book covers everything a Song general might need to know, from choosing campsites and organizing troops to building siege machines, warships and catapults.

Tucked inside are some of the earliest written recipes for gunpowder in the world. The formulas list saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal, along with other ingredients such as oils, waxes, resins and plant materials that helped the mixture stick together, burn longer or make thick smoke. Some recipes were for incendiary bombs, packages of burning powder wrapped in paper or other materials and hurled at the enemy by catapults. Others made poisonous smoke. And the book describes fire arrows, arrows carrying gunpowder that would set targets ablaze.

The original 1044 edition of the Wujing Zongyao has been lost. The oldest copy that survives today was printed in 1510, during the later Ming dynasty, so historians have to be a little careful about whether every detail and drawing matches the first version. Even so, the book shows that by the middle of the 11th century, gunpowder had moved out of the alchemist's workshop and into the official arsenals of the Chinese state, where workers produced it in large quantities.

Notice something important, though. The gunpowder in the Wujing Zongyao was mostly used for burning, not blasting or flying. The fire arrows described there were still ordinary arrows, shot from a bow, that happened to carry a burning package. The next big step would be to let the powder do the shooting itself.

sections.heading: From Burning Arrow to Flying Arrow
paragraphs: Here is a tricky puzzle for historians. Chinese writers used the same word, huojian, meaning 'fire arrow', for two very different things. One was an ordinary arrow, fired from a bow, carrying a little bundle of burning gunpowder near its tip. The other was a true rocket: an arrow that flew by itself, pushed along by a tube of gunpowder burning behind it. When an old document says that soldiers used fire arrows, it often does not tell us which kind. That is one reason it is so hard to say exactly when the first rocket flew.

The official history of the Song dynasty records that in 969 an officer named Feng Jisheng (sometimes written Feng Zhisheng) presented a new kind of fire arrow to the court, and that around the year 1000 another official, Tang Fu, presented more fire weapons. Some books say these were the first rockets. Many historians, however, think they were more likely improved incendiary arrows of the bow-shot kind. The British scientist and historian Joseph Needham, who spent decades studying the history of Chinese science, argued that the gunpowder recipes of the 11th century were not strong enough to push a rocket, and that true rockets probably did not appear before the 12th century.

How might the change from burning arrow to flying arrow have happened? The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington, DC, has a set of models that illustrate one popular theory. First came an ordinary arrow. Then came an incendiary arrow, with a tube of burning mixture tied on and pointing forward. Then, perhaps when someone noticed what happened when the gas escaped backward, came the rocket arrow, with the tube turned the other way round so that its open end faced backward. Now the jet of hot gas shot out behind, and the arrow was pushed forward, with no bow needed at all.

A rocket arrow of this kind was simple. Workers took a tube of bamboo or thick paper, packed it tightly with gunpowder, and closed off the front end. At the back they left an opening for the gas to escape, with a fuse to light it. The tube was tied to a long, thin stick, the arrow shaft, which acted like a tail. The long stick kept the rocket pointing in roughly the same direction as it flew, much like the stick on a modern firework rocket. Light the fuse, and with a hiss and a trail of sparks the arrow would leap away.

The rocket arrow works because of the principle you met in Part 1 with Hero's spinning steam ball: when the tube throws gas out of its back, the gas pushes the tube forward. Nobody in medieval China had a scientific law to describe this. They learned it by doing. And what they built was, in all the ways that matter, a genuine rocket: a vehicle carrying its own fuel and oxidizer that moves by blasting hot gas out behind it.

One clue to the rocket's birth comes not from war but from fun. In the late 12th century, Chinese writers described a firework called the dilaoshu, or 'ground rat'. It was a small tube of gunpowder that, when lit, went zooming and skittering wildly across the ground in all directions, like a frightened rat. Researchers at the Smithsonian, Frank Winter, Michael Neufeld and Kerrie Dougherty, have argued that the ground rat is the earliest device that clearly fits the definition of a true rocket, something that moves purely by its own push. There is even a famous story about one: at an imperial banquet in 1264, a ground rat firework darted towards the emperor's mother, frightening her so much that the party was stopped. These researchers suggest the rocket may have been discovered by accident, perhaps when a firework tube burst open at one end and shot away, rather than designed on purpose.

By the middle of the 1200s, the evidence becomes firm. Records describe rockets used in a Song navy exercise in 1245. From then on, rockets, or rocket arrows, appear again and again in Chinese military writing.

sections.heading: Fire Over Kaifeng, 1232
paragraphs: The most famous early story of fire arrows in battle comes from the city of Kaifeng, beside the Yellow River in northern China. Kaifeng had once been the glittering capital of the Song dynasty, one of the largest cities in the world. But in 1127 the Song lost northern China to the Jin dynasty, founded by the Jurchen people from the northeast, and the Song moved their capital south to Hangzhou. By the early 1230s, Kaifeng was the capital of the Jin.

Then a new power swept in from the steppes of Mongolia. The Mongols, united under Genghis Khan and then led by his son Ögedei, were the most feared army of the age, masters of fast horses and the bow. In 1232, a Mongol army whose generals included the famous commander Subutai surrounded Kaifeng. The siege that followed was one of the first in history in which gunpowder weapons played a major part.

The Jin defenders used several kinds of fire weapons. One was the zhentianlei, the 'thunder that shakes the heavens', an iron container packed with gunpowder that exploded with a roar people said could be heard many kilometres away. The defenders were said to lower these on chains down the city walls onto Mongol soldiers who were digging under the walls while sheltering beneath cowhide screens. Another weapon was the fire lance, a tube of gunpowder fixed to the end of a spear, which spat a jet of flame for a few moments, like a short-lived flamethrower, before the soldier used it as an ordinary spear.

And then there were what old accounts call 'arrows of flying fire', or 'flying fire lances'. Many rocket history books, including NASA's, describe these as the first recorded use of true rockets in war: tubes of gunpowder attached to long sticks, flying through the air and trailing fire. Historians are honestly not sure. The descriptions are short, and the words could also mean fire lances that shot out flames and sparks, or incendiary arrows fired from bows. It is entirely possible that some of the weapons at Kaifeng were rockets, but we cannot be certain. What we can say is that the Mongols were reportedly very frightened of these fire weapons, and that they made a deep impression.

The fire weapons did not save the city. The defenders held out for months, but famine and disease spread inside the walls, and in 1233 Kaifeng fell to the Mongols. The Jin dynasty itself came to an end the following year. The Mongols, however, had learned a valuable lesson. They began to recruit Chinese and Jurchen experts in gunpowder and siege warfare and to use these weapons themselves, carrying them across Asia as their empire grew.

sections.heading: Rockets Ride West
paragraphs: By the middle of the 1200s, the Mongol Empire stretched from Korea to the edge of Europe, the largest connected land empire the world has ever seen. Along its roads travelled merchants, diplomats, soldiers, engineers and ideas. Many historians believe this is how knowledge of gunpowder, and of rockets, spread so quickly from China to the rest of Asia and to Europe, although the exact routes are debated and written evidence is patchy.

Some of the clearest early evidence outside China comes from the Middle East. Around 1270 to 1280, a Syrian military writer named Hasan al-Rammah wrote a book about horsemanship and ingenious war devices. It contains about 107 gunpowder recipes, and 22 of them are for rockets. He also explained how to purify saltpeter using wood ashes, a crucial trick for making strong powder. His choice of words shows where the knowledge had come from: he called saltpeter 'Chinese snow' and rockets 'Chinese arrows'. Al-Rammah said he had learned much from his father and grandfathers, which suggests that gunpowder had already been known in Syria and Egypt for some time.

In Europe, the English friar and scholar Roger Bacon described a powder of saltpeter that made a loud noise and a bright flash in his work Opus Majus, written in 1267. He mentioned it being used in children's toys made in various parts of the world. Over the next century and a half, European writers described more and more rocket-like weapons. A German military engineer, Konrad Kyeser, drew several types of rockets in his book Bellifortis around 1405. An Italian engineer, Joanes de Fontana, sketched imaginative rocket-powered devices around 1420, including a rocket-driven car and a rocket torpedo meant to skim across water and set enemy ships on fire.

Meanwhile, in East Asia, rocket technology kept growing. In Korea, an official named Choe Mu-seon began producing gunpowder in the 1370s, and Korean forces built rocket weapons. By 1451, Korean engineers had created the hwacha, a wooden cart with a launching frame that could fire around a hundred rocket arrows in one terrifying volley. In China, a military manual called the Huolongjing, or 'Fire Drake Manual', from the 14th century, described all kinds of rocket weapons. One, called the 'fire dragon issuing from the water', is thought to be the earliest known two-stage rocket: a set of booster rockets carried a wooden dragon-shaped tube through the air, and when they burned out, they lit more rockets inside the dragon's mouth, which shot out towards the enemy. Ming dynasty armies also used 'wasp nest' launchers, boxes that could fire dozens of small rocket arrows at once.

These rockets were not very accurate. Many flew wildly off course, and some exploded at launch. Their real power was often in the noise, smoke and fear they caused, especially among horses. But they could be made cheaply, carried easily and fired in great numbers. Little by little, the fire arrow had become a weapon known across much of the world.

sections.heading: Sparkles in the Sky: Fireworks
paragraphs: Gunpowder was not only for war. From early on, it was also used to celebrate. Long before gunpowder, people in China threw lengths of green bamboo onto fires at New Year. As the air and moisture inside each section heated up, the bamboo burst with a loud crack. The noise was traditionally believed to scare away evil spirits and bad luck. Once gunpowder was known, people began packing it into bamboo or paper tubes to make a much louder, more reliable bang. These were the first firecrackers.

During the Song dynasty, fireworks became part of city life and celebrations. The playful ground rat was one kind. Others sputtered, sparkled or shot up into the air. Festival crowds watched entertainers set off displays, and fireworks were part of grand imperial celebrations, as the story of the frightened empress-mother at the 1264 banquet shows. Skilled fireworks makers became craftspeople in their own right.

Fireworks and rockets are close cousins. A skyrocket, the kind that whooshes up on a stick and bursts high above, is a tiny rocket: a tube of slow-burning powder that pushes it upward, carrying a small charge that bursts at the top. The same knowledge that went into war rockets also created beautiful displays, and fireworks makers were often among the most expert users of gunpowder anywhere.

As gunpowder spread west, so did the love of fireworks. By the time of the Renaissance, Italian cities were famous for spectacular displays, and later, kings and queens across Europe staged huge firework shows to celebrate victories, weddings and coronations. Today, when you watch a New Year or national holiday fireworks show and hear the crowd gasp, you are watching a tradition that began in China roughly a thousand years ago.

sections.heading: The Man on the Rocket Chair: A Legend
paragraphs: If you read about the history of rockets, sooner or later you will meet the story of Wan Hu. It is a wonderful tale, and it is told so often that many people think it is true. But it is a LEGEND, with no historical evidence behind it at all.

The story goes like this. Long ago in China, an official named Wan Hu decided to fly to the heavens. He had a sturdy chair built and fixed 47 large rockets to it, along with two big kites. On launch day, dressed in his finest robes, he sat in the chair while 47 servants, each holding a torch, rushed forward to light the fuses all at once. There was a tremendous roar and a huge cloud of smoke. When the smoke cleared, Wan Hu and his chair were gone, never to be seen again. Some say he flew to the Moon. More likely, the storytellers add, he was blown to pieces.

So where does this story come from? Not from any old Chinese book. Researchers have found no record of it in Chinese historical writing. An early forerunner of the tale appeared in the American magazine Scientific American in 1909, in which the hero was called 'Wang Tu' and the story ended with the rockets exploding. The version with the name Wan Hu and the 47 rockets was spread widely by an American author, Herbert Zim, in a 1945 book called Rockets and Jets, which gave no source for it. Joseph Needham thought the story was doubtful and might have been invented in the West. Some writers in China have since suggested a real person behind it, but no surviving evidence supports this.

The television show MythBusters tested the idea in 2004. They built a chair with rockets, using a crash-test dummy instead of a person. The result was a fiery mess, and the show concluded that such a chair would never have carried anyone very far, let alone into space. Still, the legend became so famous that in 1970 the International Astronomical Union named a crater on the far side of the Moon Wan-Hoo after him.

Why does a legend like this matter? Because it shows how easily a good story can slip into history books. Wan Hu's chair makes a great picture: a brave dreamer, a roaring blast, a mystery. But a historian's job is to ask: how do we know? Where is the evidence? For the real rockets of China, we have military books, official histories, museum reconstructions and records from many countries. For Wan Hu, we have only a story first printed in the 20th century, far from China. It is fine to enjoy it, as long as we remember it is a legend.

The real history is exciting enough. In a few hundred years, gunpowder had gone from an alchemist's accident to a weapon and a celebration known from Korea to England. Rockets would remain a common weapon for centuries, crude, loud and unpredictable. And then, in southern India, a ruler and his son would build rockets with iron casings that made them far more powerful than anything seen before.

deepDive: Two big debates surround the origins of the rocket. The first is about definitions and dates. Chinese sources use huojian ('fire arrow') both for bow-fired incendiary arrows and for self-propelled rocket arrows, so a record of 'fire arrows' in, say, 969 or 1000 does not by itself prove rockets existed. Joseph Needham, author of the monumental Science and Civilisation in China, argued that the earliest surviving gunpowder formulas, those in the Wujing Zongyao of 1044, contain too little saltpeter (around half the mixture, compared with roughly 75 percent in later European black powder) to work as an efficient propellant, and so placed true rockets no earlier than the 12th century. The first unambiguous evidence includes the 'ground rat' firework described in the late 12th century, a Song naval exercise of 1245 and the 1264 banquet incident. Smithsonian historians Frank Winter, Michael Neufeld and Kerrie Dougherty go further, suggesting the rocket was not deliberately invented at all but discovered by accident, perhaps when a firework tube vented from one end and skittered away. The 1232 'flying fire' at Kaifeng is often cited as the first battlefield use of rockets, but the Chinese term (fei huo qiang) can also be read as a fire lance, a hand-held flame-spewing tube, so many specialists treat Kaifeng as possible rather than proven. The second debate concerns how gunpowder spread. One school, represented by historians such as Tonio Andrade and Stephen Haw, sees the Mongol Empire as 'the first gunpowder empire', moving Chinese technicians and techniques across Eurasia. Others, such as Kate Raphael, point out how thin the written evidence for Mongol transmission actually is. What is not in doubt is the direction of travel: the vocabulary of Hasan al-Rammah, who called saltpeter 'Chinese snow' and rockets 'Chinese arrows', and the relatively late dates of the first Middle Eastern (about 1240 to 1280) and European (Roger Bacon, 1267) formulas all point back to China. The underlying chemistry also explains the slow pace of progress. Saltpeter must be purified, typically by dissolving it, treating it with wood ash to remove calcium and magnesium salts and recrystallizing it, before powder becomes strong and reliable. Each improvement in purification and proportion made rockets more powerful.
funFact: A crater on the far side of the Moon is officially named Wan-Hoo after the man in the rocket-chair legend, even though there is no evidence he ever existed.
